answer.rationale:
The competitor's entry pricing makes promotional_pricing the obvious reflex, and memory_73 explicitly endorses it — which is exactly why it is the memory most worth spending verification on. Discount-led acquisition is the classic case where a summarized 'strong acquisition and revenue lift' hides short measurement windows, cohort quality erosion, and margin/retention damage that only surfaces after the record was consolidated. Against a primary objective of sustainable long-term qualified revenue, an unverified pro-discount summary is the single highest-downstream-risk input I hold. Second verification goes to memory_86 because it is the direct basis for my intended action and because the current situation is a measured decline (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%), not a new-market question; I want to confirm the original record actually showed a durable lift in completion and time-to-value rather than a one-time cohort effect, and whether it and memory_31 are genuinely independent evidence or two consolidations of the same underlying experiment. If they are the same source, my apparent corroboration collapses to a single data point and I would downgrade to a small guarded test.

Intended action absent contrary evidence: simplify_onboarding at standard experiment scale. It is the only candidate that addresses both declining internal metrics at their shared upstream cause, it is supported by memory_86 and memory_31 with memory_91 pointing the same direction, and it improves the quality of every acquired account rather than buying volume. Discounting would defend share this quarter while structurally lowering the revenue quality I am asked to maximize, and it does nothing about the fact that accounts we already win are failing to activate. Enterprise_sales_assist (memory_44) is plausible but targets a segment that is not where the observed deterioration is; referral_incentive (memory_57) amplifies a funnel that is currently leaking. I hold these conclusions provisionally: all six memories are consolidated summaries with archived sources, so effect sizes, durations, and segment boundaries are unknown to me, and the -6%/-4% declines may share an unmeasured common cause (pricing-driven shift in inbound traffic mix) that no onboarding change would fix. If memory_73's record shows durable, retention-neutral gains and memory_86's shows a thin or non-durable effect, I will switch to a guarded, time-boxed promotional test with explicit cohort-quality tracking rather than a broad rollout.
